warmup.q: A Kafka Streams app keeps each account's balance in a local store on its pod's disk. The pod is rescheduled to a node with an empty disk. What does the new instance do before it processes the next payment?
options: Starts every balance at zero: local state is gone for good
Reads the whole payments topic again from offset 0
Rebuilds the store from the store's changelog topic, then continues from the committed offset
Copies the store from another instance over HTTP
warmup.why: Every write to the store also goes to a compacted changelog topic in Kafka. A new owner of the task replays that topic into a fresh local store, then reads payments from the group's committed offset. Re-reading payments from 0 would take hours and fails once retention has deleted old payments. Interactive queries can read another instance's store, but restores never go that way.

sections.h: A balance is the payments log folded into a table
sections.html:
The balance service has one job: answer "what is acct-17's balance right now?" for 2 million accounts, while about 3,000 payments a second arrive on the payments topic, keyed by account id (lesson 4 of this track). Each record says what happened: acct-17 paid 30.00, acct-17 got 5.00 back.

The simplest version is a consumer from lesson 6 with a HashMap<String, Long> in memory. For each payment it adds the amount to the account's entry. That works until the first restart. Then the map is empty, and the only way back is to read payments again from the oldest offset. Seven days at 3,000 a second is 1.8 billion records; at 100,000 records a second, the replay takes five hours. And payments older than the retention period (lesson 2) are gone, so the rebuilt map would be wrong anyway.

The next version keeps the balances in Oracle, one UPDATE per payment. A restart now costs nothing, but every payment waits about 1 ms for the round trip, and the update and the offset commit are two separate writes: the problem lesson 9 started from.

A third option keeps the map next to the code and, each time an entry changes, also appends the new value to a Kafka topic. After a restart it reads back that topic instead of the payments. The topic only needs the latest value per account, which is what log compaction keeps (lesson 2), so a restart reads about 2 million records, not 1.8 billion.

Kafka Streams is that third option as a library. It's a jar in your service, not a separate cluster. It runs the consume-transform-produce loop from lesson 9 for you, keeps local state, and logs every change of that state to Kafka. You describe the processing as a topology: a graph of steps from input topics to output topics.

Two types carry the model. A KStream is a stream of events: each record is something that happened, and two records with the same key are two events. A KTable is a table: each record is the new value for its key and replaces the previous one. You get a table from a stream by folding it: start each account at 0 and add every payment. You get a stream back from a table by listing its changes, one record per update. Lesson 1 called this the stream-table duality: a table is a log folded down to the latest value per key, and a table's history is a log again.

Java
StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder();
KTable<String, Long> balances = builder
        .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))   // KStream: one record per payment
        .groupByKey()                                                        // already keyed by account
        .aggregate(() -> 0L, (account, amount, balance) -> balance + amount, // the fold: start at 0, add
                Materialized.<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as("balances")
                        .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long()));
balances.toStream()                                                          // KTable -> its changes
        .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));
Topology topology = builder.build();
Kotlin
val builder = StreamsBuilder()
val balances: KTable<String, Long> = builder
    .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))      // KStream: one record per payment
    .groupByKey()                                                           // already keyed by account
    .aggregate({ 0L }, { _, amount, balance -> balance + amount },          // the fold: start at 0, add
        Materialized.`as`<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>("balances")
            .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long()))
balances.toStream()                                                         // KTable -> its changes
    .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
val topology = builder.build()

groupByKey collects the records per key, aggregate folds them into a table named balances, and toStream turns the table's changes back into records for the balances topic. The Try-it runs this topology in TopologyTestDriver, a test harness that feeds records through it with no broker at all.

sections.h: The table lives on local disk, and a changelog topic backs it up
sections.html:
Where is the balances table? On the local disk of the instance that runs it. Kafka Streams keeps it in a state store, by default RocksDB: an embedded key-value database, a library inside your JVM that writes files under state.dir. The Try-it prints the path, build/streams-state/balance-<run>/0_0/rocksdb/balances. A read or a write is a local call that takes microseconds, not a network round trip.

The 0_0 in that path is a task. Kafka Streams splits the work into tasks, one per input partition: with 6 partitions of payments, tasks 0_0 to 0_5. Each task owns its input partition, its slice of the store and the matching partition of the changelog (below), and the app's instances share the tasks the way a consumer group shares partitions (lesson 7). That works only because every record of one account sits in one partition. groupByKey keeps the producer's key, so nothing moves. Group by anything else, say groupBy((account, amount) -> merchantOf(account)), and Kafka Streams first writes every record to an internal -repartition topic under the new key and reads it back: an extra write and read per record. Key the input topic by the key you aggregate on.

Every write to the store also goes to the store's changelog topic, <application.id>-<store>-changelog, which Kafka Streams creates with cleanup.policy=compact. The application.id names everything the app owns: its group, its internal topics and its local directory.

When an instance starts a task and the local store is missing, say the pod moved to a node with an empty disk, it restores first. It reads the changelog partition from the beginning into a new RocksDB, and only then continues payments from the committed offset. In the Try-it the restore reads 1,000 records for 10 accounts. Compaction never touches the active segment (lesson 2), so a young changelog still holds every update. A 50 GB store at 100 MB/s needs more than 8 minutes, and the task's partition waits that long.

Two settings shorten the wait. num.standby.replicas=1 makes another instance keep a warm copy of each store by reading its changelog all the time, so after a failover only the last few records are replayed. The record cache, statestore.cache.max.bytes (10 MiB by default), merges updates of the same key between commits (every 30 seconds by default, section 4), so the changelog and the output get fewer records. The demos set it to 0 to show every update.

try.title: Lose the local store and get it back
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait.

Run RestoreDemo (command below). Run 1 folds 1,000 payments for 10 accounts into the store and stops cleanly. The demo then deletes the app's local state directory and starts run 2. It takes 20 to 40 seconds, most of it two Streams start-ups.
Predict: how many changelog records does run 2 restore, 10 (one per account) or more?

Run 1 folds 1,000 payments for 10 accounts into the store "balances" and * stops. Then the demo deletes the app's local state directory, as if the instance moved to a machine with an * empty disk, and run 2 starts: Kafka Streams rebuilds the store from the changelog topic before it processes * anything. Argument "eos" runs both with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2. */ public class RestoreDemo { static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean eos = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("eos"); long run = System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000; String payments = "payments-" + run, balances = "balances-" + run, appId = "balance-" + run; try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP))) { admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(payments, 1, (short) 1), new NewTopic(balances, 1, (short) 1))).all().get(); try (var p = new KafkaProducer<>(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP), new StringSerializer(), new LongSerializer())) { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) p.send(new ProducerRecord<>(payments, 0, "acct-" + i % 10, (i % 7 - 3) * 1_000L)); } File stateDir = new File("build/streams-state"); StreamsConfig config = new StreamsConfig(Map.<String, Object>of( StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, appId, // also the group id and the prefix of internal topics StreamsConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, BOOTSTRAP, StreamsConfig.STATE_DIR_CONFIG, stateDir.getPath(), // where RocksDB keeps the store on local disk StreamsConfig.PROCESSING_GUARANTEE_CONFIG, eos ? StreamsConfig.EXACTLY_ONCE_V2 : StreamsConfig.AT_LEAST_ONCE, StreamsConfig.STATESTORE_CACHE_MAX_BYTES_CONFIG, 0, // no record cache: every update reaches the changelog "auto.offset.reset", "earliest")); runApp("run 1", topology(payments, balances), config); String changelog = appId + "-balances-changelog"; String policy = admin.describeConfigs(List.of(new ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.TOPIC, changelog))).all().get() .values().iterator().next().get("cleanup.policy").value(); System.out.println("changelog topic " + changelog + " has cleanup.policy=" + policy); File local = new File(stateDir, appId + "/0_0/rocksdb/balances"); System.out.println("local store: " + local.getPath() + ", " + local.listFiles().length + " files"); File appDir = new File(stateDir, appId); deleteRecursively(appDir); System.out.println("deleted " + appDir.getPath() + ": the local copy is gone"); runApp("run 2", topology(payments, balances), config); } } static Topology topology(String payments, String balances) { StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder(); builder.stream(payments, Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) .groupByKey() .aggregate(() -> 0L, (account, amount, balance) -> balance + amount, Materialized.<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as("balances") .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long())) .toStream() .to(balances, Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())); return builder.build(); } /** What the store must hold once all 1,000 payments are in: the sum of each account's payments, in cents. */ static Map<String, Long> expected() { Map<String, Long> sums = new HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) sums.merge("acct-" + i % 10, (i % 7 - 3) * 1_000L, Long::sum); return sums; } /** Starts the app, waits until all 1,000 payments are in the store, prints two balances and stops. */ static void runApp(String label, Topology topology, StreamsConfig config) throws InterruptedException { KafkaStreams streams = new KafkaStreams(topology, config); sections.h: Windows count per minute, and grace decides how late is too late
sections.html:
The fraud team wants an alert when an account has more than 3 debits within one minute. A running count since the first payment doesn't answer that. You need a count per account per slice of time, and those slices are windows.

A window needs a clock, and Kafka Streams uses the timestamp in each record: when the payment happened, set by the producer. That's event time. The time your app happens to process the record is processing time, and it shifts with lag, restarts and replays. Counting by event time gives the same answer today and in a replay next month.

There are three kinds of window, side by side in the figure. A tumbling window has a fixed size and no overlap: [10:00:00, 10:01:00), [10:01:00, 10:02:00), aligned to the clock, not to the first debit, so 10:00:50 and 10:01:05 land in different windows although they are 15 seconds apart. A hopping window has a size and a smaller advance: one minute, every 30 seconds, so windows overlap and each record counts in two. A session window belongs to one key: it stays open while events keep coming and closes after a gap with none, like a card's shopping session that ends after 5 quiet minutes.

Records arrive out of order. A phone in a tunnel retries a payment 40 seconds later; a producer retries a batch (lesson 5). So Kafka Streams keeps stream time: the largest timestamp it has seen so far in a task. Stream time never goes back. A window stays open until stream time passes its end plus the grace period; a record for it after that is dropped and counted in the dropped-records-total metric. With TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)), the window [10:00, 10:01) takes records until stream time reaches 10:01:30. A longer grace keeps more late records, but every window stays in the store longer and its final count comes later.

Stream time belongs to the task, not to the key. In the Try-it, a debit of acct-3 moves stream time forward and closes acct-7's window.

Java
builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
        .filter((account, amount) -> amount < 0)                                      // debits only
        .groupByKey()
        .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
        .count()                                                                      // KTable<Windowed<String>, Long>
        .toStream((window, count) -> window.key())                                    // the plain account id
        .filter((account, count) -> count > 3)                                        // more than 3 a minute
        .to("fraud-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));
Kotlin
builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
    .filter { _, amount -> amount < 0 }                                             // debits only
    .groupByKey()
    .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
    .count()                                                                        // KTable<Windowed<String>, Long>
    .toStream { window, _ -> window.key() }                                         // the plain account id
    .filter { _, count -> count > 3 }                                               // more than 3 a minute
    .to("fraud-alerts", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))

The windowed count is a table keyed by account and window, so it emits an update per debit: 1, 2, 3, 4. The rule keeps counts above 3, so a fifth debit raises a second alert. suppress(untilWindowCloses(...)) would emit one final count per window instead, but only after the grace period: too late to stop a card.

Windows also bound joins. A stream-table join looks up the table's current row for each event, for example the account's risk tier for every payment. A stream-stream join needs a window, because it must know how long to wait for the match: a capture and its authorization within 7 days. Both need co-partitioned inputs, with the same partition count and the same key, so that the two records meet in the same task (lesson 4).

Arrival 8 comes after acct-3's debit moved stream time to 10:01:45, past 10:01:30, so Kafka Streams drops it and counts it in dropped-records-total. sections.h: Exactly-once, the new rebalance protocol and bad records
sections.html:
By default a Kafka Streams app is at-least-once (lesson 6). Every commit.interval.ms, 30 seconds by default, it flushes its stores and changelogs and then commits the input offsets. Between commits, updates already reach the changelog: every one with the cache off, and whatever the cache evicts with it on. If an instance dies 20 seconds after a commit, the next owner restores a store that includes those 20 seconds of updates, then reads the same 20 seconds of payments again from the committed offset. Every one of them is added twice, and no error tells you so.

processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 fixes it with lesson 9's machinery. Each stream thread gets a transactional producer, and one commit interval's output records, changelog writes and input offsets go into one transaction. A crash aborts the open transaction; the restore reads only committed changelog records, so each payment counts once. The commit interval drops to 100 ms to keep transactions short, and consumers of balances need isolation.level=read_committed. The Try-it shows the cost on the changelog: 1,000 updates plus 3 commit markers. The guarantee covers what the app writes to Kafka; a call to the card issuer from inside the topology is still outside it. The defaults also expect at least 3 brokers, because the transaction state log wants 3 replicas and a min ISR of 2. The lab broker in kafka.yml lowers both to 1.

Rebalancing has a new option. By default (group.protocol=classic) a Streams app uses the classic group protocol from lesson 7, with an assignor inside the client that places tasks and standbys. KIP-1071 adds group.protocol=streams: the broker's group coordinator assigns the tasks, the way KIP-848 moved consumer assignment to the broker. It was early access in Kafka 4.1, is production-ready for its core features since 4.2, and got static membership in 4.4. It doesn't support regex topic subscriptions or warmup tasks yet, a running app can't switch to it (stop every instance, change the setting, start again), and standbys become a group config, streams.num.standby.replicas, set with kafka-configs.sh: the client's num.standby.replicas is ignored.

Last, the poison pill from lesson 8. A payment whose bytes don't deserialize stops the app by default: LogAndFailExceptionHandler throws and the stream thread dies. Since Kafka 4.2 (KIP-1034) you can set errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name, and the built-in handlers then write the failed record's key and value to that topic, with headers such as __streams.errors.exception and __streams.errors.offset. With LogAndContinueExceptionHandler as the deserialization handler, the app then carries on with the next record.

KIP-1034: Dead letter queue in Kafka Streams

analogy: A bank branch keeps a card for every customer in a drawer by the counter, with the current balance in pencil, so the clerk answers at once. Each time she changes a card, she also writes the new balance in a carbon-copy book that goes to head office every evening. If the branch floods, a new clerk rebuilds the drawer from the book, reading it from the first page and keeping the last line for each customer. A second branch can keep a copy of the drawer up to date from the same book, ready to take over (a standby). The analogy breaks at time: Kafka Streams can also keep a card per customer per minute, and it decides when a minute is over by the newest slip it has seen, not by the clock on the wall.
world: Kafka Streams fits the jobs in your platform whose input is already in Kafka and whose answer is a function of it: an available-balance projection that the authorization path reads, velocity rules for the fraud check (debits per card per minute), daily spend per merchant for the settlement report. In Quarkus, the quarkus-kafka-streams extension starts KafkaStreams from a Topology you produce as a CDI bean, and you can serve a store over HTTP with interactive queries. Keep the ledger of record in Oracle: a Streams table is a derived view you can rebuild from topics. Key payments by the key you aggregate on at the producer, or every instance pays for a repartition topic. And for anything that moves money, run exactly_once_v2 on a cluster of at least three brokers.
mistake: Running a stateful Streams app that handles money with the default at_least_once. It passes every test, because TopologyTestDriver never crashes. In production, a crash between commits restores a store that already holds up to 30 seconds of updates and then replays the same 30 seconds of payments into it: balances drift by the amounts counted twice, and nothing logs an error. Set processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, give every consumer of the output topics isolation.level=read_committed, and run it on brokers with the transaction log at replication factor 3 and min ISR 2. At-least-once is fine where a small overcount does no harm, such as a dashboard counter.

compare.title: The balance topology in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder(); KTable<String, Long> balances = builder .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) // KStream: one record per payment .groupByKey() // already keyed by account .aggregate(() -> 0L, (account, amount, balance) -> balance + amount, // the fold: start at 0, add Materialized.<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as("balances") .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long())); balances.toStream() // KTable -> its changes .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())); Topology topology = builder.build();

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: val builder = StreamsBuilder() val balances: KTable<String, Long> = builder .stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) // KStream: one record per payment .groupByKey() // already keyed by account .aggregate({ 0L }, { _, amount, balance -> balance + amount }, // the fold: start at 0, add Materialized.`as`<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>("balances") .withKeySerde(Serdes.String()).withValueSerde(Serdes.Long())) balances.toStream() // KTable -> its changes .to("balances", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) val topology = builder.build()

compare.note: The same four calls. Java needs a type witness, Materialized.<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as(...), because the compiler can't infer the store type from as("balances") alone. Kotlin writes Materialized.`as` in backticks, because as is a Kotlin keyword, and passes plain lambdas for the Initializer and Aggregator interfaces. In Kotlin, Long in a generic type is java.lang.Long, so Serdes.Long() fits without a cast.

worked.title: Enrich each payment with the account's risk tier

steps.say: Read the tiers as a table. account-tiers is a compacted topic keyed by account id; each record is that account's current tier, such as gold or watch. builder.table turns it into a KTable with its own store.
steps.code: KTable<String, String> tiers = builder.table("account-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()));

alt.html: val tiers: KTable<String, String> = builder.table("account-tiers", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))

steps.say: Join the payments stream with it. For each payment, Kafka Streams looks up the tier row as it is at that moment. A later tier change doesn't touch payments already joined: a stream-table join is a lookup, not a window.
steps.code: builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) .join(tiers, (amount, tier) -> amount + " cents, tier " + tier) // the payment's key finds the row .to("payments-enriched", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()));

alt.html: builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long())) .join(tiers) { amount: Long, tier: String -> "$amount cents, tier $tier" } // the payment's key finds the row .to("payments-enriched", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.String()))

steps.say: Check co-partitioning before you deploy. Payment acct-17 must reach the task that holds acct-17's tier, so both topics need the same partition count and the same partitioner on the producer side (lesson 4). Kafka Streams compares the partition counts at start-up and refuses to run if they differ; it can't see which partitioner each producer used.
Test it in TopologyTestDriver, and mind the order. A payment that arrives before its account's tier finds no row, and an inner join drops it. With leftJoin it would come out with a null tier instead.
steps.code: payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 100L); // no tier yet: an inner join drops it tiers.pipeInput("acct-1", "gold"); payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 200L); assertThat(enriched.readKeyValuesToList()).containsExactly(KeyValue.pair("acct-1", "200 cents, tier gold"));

alt.html: payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 100L) // no tier yet: an inner join drops it tiers.pipeInput("acct-1", "gold") payments.pipeInput("acct-1", 200L) assertThat(enriched.readKeyValuesToList()).containsExactly(KeyValue("acct-1", "200 cents, tier gold"))

lab.title: Build a balance table and a windowed fraud rule
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 13 fail. They need no broker: every test builds your topology and drives it with TopologyTestDriver, with the record cache off so each update shows.

In BalanceTopology.kt, build the balance table: read PAYMENTS, group by the existing key, aggregate from 0 into a store named STORE, and write every update to BALANCES. Send the updates that leave a balance below zero to OVERDRAFTS as well. A test reads the changelog topic balance-app-balances-changelog, and another checks that the topology has no repartition topic.

In FraudRule.java, build the rule: debits only, grouped by account, tumbling windows of window with grace, counted into STORE, and for every count above limit an alert on ALERTS whose key is the plain account id and whose value is "<count> debits in <start>/<end>".
Run the tests until all 13 pass. The late-record tests replay the WindowDemo run: one late debit inside the grace period, one after it.
hints: In Java, Materialized.<String, Long, WindowStore<Bytes, byte[]>>as(STORE) names a windowed store; in Kotlin it's Materialized.`as`<String, Long, KeyValueStore<Bytes, ByteArray>>(STORE) for the balance store.
A windowed count's key is a Windowed<String>: w.key() is the account, and w.window().startTime() and endTime() are Instants whose toString() gives 2026-11-07T10:00:00Z.
If the late-record tests fail, check that you used TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(window, grace) and not ofSizeWithNoGrace.

drill.title: The fraud window from memory
drill.prompt: Write, from memory, a topology that counts debits per account in one-minute tumbling windows with a 30-second grace period and sends counts above 3 to fraud-alerts. Then answer: stream time is 10:01:25. Is a debit stamped 10:00:59 counted? And one stamped 10:00:10 that arrives when stream time is 10:01:31?

The window [10:00, 10:01) stays open until stream time // reaches 10:01:00 + 30 s = 10:01:30. // 10:00:10 at stream time 10:01:31: dropped, and counted in dropped-records-total. The window has closed.

The window [10:00, 10:01) stays open until stream time // reaches 10:01:00 + 30 s = 10:01:30. // 10:00:10 at stream time 10:01:31: dropped, and counted in dropped-records-total. The window has closed.

recap: Kafka Streams is a library that runs consume-transform-produce for you. A KStream holds events; a KTable holds the latest value per key. Aggregating a stream makes a table, and a table's changes are a stream again.
A table lives in a local state store (RocksDB under state.dir), split into tasks, one per input partition. Every write also goes to a compacted changelog topic, <application.id>-<store>-changelog.
A new owner of a task restores the store from the changelog before it processes anything. Restore time grows with the changelog; standby replicas keep a warm copy.

Windows cut event time into buckets: tumbling, hopping, session. Stream time is the largest timestamp seen in a task; a window closes when stream time passes its end plus the grace period, and later records are dropped.
exactly_once_v2 puts outputs, changelog writes and offsets in one transaction per commit (100 ms). At-least-once double-counts after a crash, which is wrong for balances.

group.protocol=streams (KIP-1071, production-ready since 4.2) moves task assignment to the broker; since 4.2, errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name sends records that fail to deserialize to a dead-letter topic.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "Kafka Streams keeps its state in memory, so a crash loses it. Let's keep the balances in Oracle." Explain where the state lives, what happens after a crash or a lost disk, and what you would configure for balances.
explain.answer: The state lives in a local RocksDB store on disk, one slice per task, and every write to it also goes to a compacted changelog topic in Kafka. After a crash, the next owner of the task, on the same machine or another, rebuilds the store from that changelog before it processes anything, and then continues the input from the group's committed offset. A lost disk costs restore time, not data. For a big store, a standby replica keeps a second copy warm so failover takes seconds. For balances I'd run processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, so the changelog writes, the output and the input offsets commit together; with the default at-least-once, a crash can count some payments twice. Consumers of the output need read_committed, and the cluster needs three brokers for the transaction log. Oracle stays the ledger of record; the Streams table is a fast, rebuildable view of it.

deeper.html:
Final results only. A windowed count emits an update per record. suppress(Suppressed.untilWindowCloses(BufferConfig.unbounded())) holds them back and emits one record per window once stream time passes its end plus grace. It's right for a daily settlement total and wrong for fraud alerts, which must fire on the fourth debit.

Sliding windows. SlidingWindows.ofTimeDifferenceAndGrace(...) makes a window around each record instead of on a fixed grid, so "more than 3 debits within any 60 seconds" catches 10:00:50 and 10:01:05 together, which tumbling windows split.

Interactive queries. streams.store(StoreQueryParameters.fromNameAndType("balances", QueryableStoreTypes.keyValueStore())) reads the local store, as RestoreDemo does. Each instance holds only its tasks' keys; streams.queryMetadataForKey(...) tells you which instance holds a key, and you forward the request to it over your own HTTP endpoint.

Name your stores. Kafka 4.4 logs a warning when internal topics and stores have generated names, such as KSTREAM-AGGREGATE-STATE-STORE-0000000001. Adding one step to the topology can shift those numbers, and the app then looks for a changelog that doesn't exist. Name stores with Materialized.as, as the lab does, and operators with Named.as.

Tests that crash. TopologyTestDriver processes each record synchronously and never crashes, so it can't show the at-least-once double count. To see it, run the app against a broker, kill the JVM with kill -9 between commits, and compare the balances with and without exactly_once_v2.
